newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzanian airline head sets privatisation deadline.
newsitem.headline: Tanzanian airline head sets privatisation deadline.

text.p: Tanzania's state-owned national carrier, Air Tanzania Corporation (ATC), aims to be privatised before the end of 1998, ATC Chairman Abbas Sykes told Reuters on Sunday.

Sykes said a coalition of Malaysian investors had signalled their interest in aquiring a share of the airline once it was offered for sale. He said he would also seek talks with Germany's national carrier Lufthansa to determine any interest in a joint venture.
"We (ATC) are eager to bring in the same approach as Kenya Airways and Dutch KLM. It (KLM) is a senior airline," he said.

In 1996 KLM aquired a 26 percent stake in Kenya Airways, a move which brought an economic turnaround for the cash strapped carrier. Critics of the deal say Kenya Airways now ceases to exist with all strategic decisions taken by KLM.
Sykes said moves to attract British Airways as a partner were unsuccessful. "They are not interested. They don't need us because they are quite comfortable where they are," he said.

The ATC chairman reaffirmed his opposition to a merger involving Alliance Airlines in which the Tanzanian and Ugandan government each hold a 30 percent stake with the remaining equity held by South African Airways.

Syke's comments were at odds with Tanzanian transport minister William Kusila's statement to parliament on July 24 in which he said a consultant had been appointed to investigate the feasibility of a merger between Uganda Airlines, ATC and Alliance, "in order to take advantage of economies of scale and efficiency."

"Alliance is not viable. They don't own a plane - they've just leased one. It (Alliance) has been making losses ever since it came into being - now more than $25 million," Sykes said adding: he feared a deal with Alliance would pave the way for South African domination of sub-Saharan skies.
"I think the whole thing is political. The way I see it the South African business people want to control the entire market of Africa south of the Sahara.
"They want to take everything and turn black Africa into a South African market which is really a market for the European Union and the United States," he said.
He said ATC, owners of two Boeing 737-200s and two Fokker F- 27 turbo-props, had shown a modest profit for each financial year since economic reforms were implemented in 1992.

"In the first fiscal year we had a small profit and in 1993/ 94 we made 384 million shillings ($622,000), in 1994/95 we made 600 million shillings and 750 million in 1996/97. This year (1997/98) we expect to make even more."
